name: Middle Low German

ancestors.notes: Descent per Glottolog classification of Middle Low German (midd1318).

notes: Research. West Germanic (Ingvaeonic/Low Saxon) medieval stage written in the Latin alphabet. Grapheme map covers the basic vowels, doubled long vowels, the digraphs sch [ʃ], ch [x], ng and ck, and the plain consonants with v and w both mapped to [v]. Middle Low German spelling was not standardised across the Hanseatic writing tradition; vowel length and quality were marked inconsistently and are largely left unencoded, so a notable PER floor is expected. Grapheme table checked against Lasch (1914): no discrepancy found. `positional_graphemes.e` encodes the reduction of unstressed non-initial-syllable vowels (mostly historical short a/i/o/u of medial and final syllables) to a single schwa-like sound, normally spelled <e>, that Lasch (1914) describes for the medial/final-syllable vowel system (§§211-212: 'Die im as. noch vorhandene Mannigfaltigkeit der kurzen Vokale in den unbetonten Silben hat sich mnd. auf einen meist durch e wiedergegebenen Laut reduziert', p. 116-117); the gold cache confirms this is realised as [ə] in practice (e.g. all 58 -en-final polysyllables and the large majority of -e-final polysyllables in the wikipron sample). Word-final obstruent devoicing was checked against the gold and could not be evaluated: the 143-word sample contains no orthographically b- or d-final word and only one g-final word, too little evidence to source a rule either way.

stress.notes: Middle Low German, like other West Germanic varieties of its period, keeps the inherited Common Germanic fixed root-initial stress (Lasch 1914). `default_position=1` (first syllable) models this; stress-neutral prefixes and loanwords are not separately handled for lack of a documented closed list in the sources consulted.
